Participants were asked to answer via button press offline (after taking off the fNIRS cap) for each run (20 questions total) to verify attention to the task and comprehension of the story.
To promote comfort with task demands, participants were first provided with verbal instructions prior to completing a practice task.
Individuals with aphasia and age-matched participants were additionally provided with a pictorial version of the instructions.
Participants were then given an opportunity to ask questions about task completion.
The practice task could be completed as many times as necessary until participants were comfortable with the task.
For four participants with clinical MRIs, the scans were reviewed and general lesion location was confirmed.
All participants completed a fiveminute resting trial prior to the experimental task.
The racial and ethnic composition of the young neurotypical individuals was reflective of the university population from which they were recruited.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.formatted: The processing stream included 1) pruning of channels with SNR < 5 dB; 2) conversion of raw light intensity data to optical density; 3) motion artifact correction using a spline interpolation method with Savitsky-Golay filtering (frame size = 10 seconds; p = .99; <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Jahani et al., 2018)</ref>; 4) lowpass filtering to remove high-frequency noise (filter frequency = of 0.5 Hz); 5) conversion of optical density to concentration units using the modified Beer-Lambert Law without path-length correction; and 6) estimation of the hemodynamic response function using a generalized linear model at the run level for changes in HbO and HbR across the block time course with short separation regression (using the short separation channel with the greatest correlation to each channel) and signal drift correction (trange = -2 to 20 seconds; <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Huppert et al., 2009)</ref>.
table.expanded: The processing stream included 1) pruning of channels with SNR < 5 dB; 2) conversion of raw light intensity data to optical density; 3) motion artifact correction using a spline interpolation method with Savitsky-Golay filtering (frame size = 10 seconds; p = .99; Jahani et al., 2018); 4) lowpass filtering to remove high-frequency noise (filter frequency = of 0.5 Hz); 5) conversion of optical density to concentration units using the modified Beer-Lambert Law without path-length correction; and 6) estimation of the hemodynamic response function using a generalized linear model at the run level for changes in HbO and HbR across the block time course with short separation regression (using the short separation channel with the greatest correlation to each channel) and signal drift correction (trange = -2 to 20 seconds; Huppert et al., 2009).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .99", "p = .91", "p = .646", "p > .05", "p > .05"), Sentence = c("The processing stream included 1) pruning of channels with SNR < 5 dB; 2) conversion of raw light intensity data to optical density; 3) motion artifact correction using a spline interpolation method with Savitsky-Golay filtering (frame size = 10 seconds; p = .99; Jahani et al., 2018); 4) lowpass filtering to remove high-frequency noise (filter frequency = of 0.5 Hz); 5) conversion of optical density to concentration units using the modified Beer-Lambert Law without path-length correction; and 6) estimation of the hemodynamic response function using a generalized linear model at the run level for changes in HbO and HbR across the block time course with short separation regression (using the short separation channel with the greatest correlation to each channel) and signal drift correction (trange = -2 to 20 seconds; Huppert et al., 2009).", "Follow-up pairwise comparison showed that the young neurotypical group had greater HbO for narrative vs. counting (adjusted p = .005) that was not seen in the age-matched group (adjusted p = .91).", "Follow-up pairwise comparison showed greater HbO for narrative vs. counting for the young neurotypical group (adjusted p < .001) and the individuals with aphasia (adjusted p < .001) that was not seen in the age-matched group (adjusted p = .646).", "Exploratory ROIs: There were no significant interactions or effects of group or condition in bilateral parietal ROIs (all unadjusted p > .05).", "Although follow-up pairwise comparison did not show any significant differences after multiple comparison correction (all adjusted p > .05), the trend was toward individuals with aphasia showing greater cortical activity for counting than narrative." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Boston University and all participants provided written informed consent prior to study participation.
live_data_statements: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Boston University and all participants provided written informed consent prior to study participation.

Participants were 14 young neurotypical adults (mean age = 23.5 years, SD = 4.1), 17 individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia (mean age = 61.6, SD = 9.2), and 15 age-matched neurotypical adults (mean age = 59.5 years, SD = 9.6).
Young neurotypical individuals (6 female; 8 male) were recruited from a university setting (See Table 1 for individual demographics for the young neurotypical group).

Table 1: Young Neurotypical Participant Demographics ID Age Sex Handedness Race Ethnicity Native Language Other Languages Years Education Y1 male R white NH English -14 Y2 male R white Hispanic English Spanish 14 Y3 female R white NH English Russian 20 Y4 male R white NH English French* 19 Y5 female R Asian NH English Korean 13 Y6 female R white NH English Italian* 19 Y7 female R Asian NH English Korean 15 Y8 female R white NH English -18 Y9 male R Asian Hispanic English Spanish 13 Y10 female R Black NH Igbo English 20 Y12 male R white Hispanic English Spanish 16 Y13 male Ambidextrous Black NH English French, Patois 15 Y14 male R Asian NH English Urdu 18 Y15 male R white Hispanic English Spanish, Danish, Japanese 15 Mean 23.5 *basic 16.4 SD 4.2 2.6 NH: non-Hispanic Age-matched neurotypical participants (9 female; 6 male) were recruited via contacting individuals from an existing database in the Center for Brain Recovery at Boston University and through self-referral to the Center for Brain Recovery (See Table 2 for individual demographics for the age-matched group).

Individuals with aphasia (4 female; 13 male) were recruited from an existing database in the Center for Brain Recovery at Boston University as well as through contacting local clinicians, aphasia groups, and community groups (see Table 3 for individual demographics for the individuals with aphasia).
Ethnicityall participants were non-Hispanic; Native languagenative language English for all participants
Participants were asked to answer via button press offline (after taking off the fNIRS cap) for each run (20 questions total) to verify attention to the task and comprehension of the story.
To promote comfort with task demands, participants were first provided with verbal instructions prior to completing a practice task.
Individuals with aphasia and age-matched participants were additionally provided with a pictorial version of the instructions.
Participants were then given an opportunity to ask questions about task completion.
The practice task could be completed as many times as necessary until participants were comfortable with the task.
For four participants with clinical MRIs, the scans were reviewed and general lesion location was confirmed.
All participants completed a fiveminute resting trial prior to the experimental task.
The racial and ethnic composition of the young neurotypical individuals was reflective of the university population from which they were recruited.
